title: Hyperloom Systems — Partner intro & onramp framing
summary: Introductory partner discovery between Redwood and Hyperloom Systems to explore channel integration for hybrid GPU onramp, routing patterns, and enterprise security requirements. Key themes: Dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs, VPC/private deployment constraints, latency targets for inference, and next steps to run a benchmark and share security/compliance artifacts.

Priya Menon — share internal traffic profile and 99th percentile latency targets — due 2026-12-02

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-29
Start time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Claire Jensen (Redwood AE), Marco Alvarez (Redwood SE), Tanya Li (Redwood Partnerships), Priya Menon (Hyperloom Head of Platform), Liam O'Connor (CTO), Jae Park (Infra Eng), Rana Issa (Security)

[00:00:02] Claire: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. This is Claire from Redwood — I'm the account lead on partner programs. Marco is our systems SE, Tanya from partnerships is here to help with partner model framing. Quick round robin?
[00:00:15] Priya: Hi, I'm Priya, Head of Platform at Hyperloom Systems. We're exploring a GPU onramp to offer managed inference to customers; we resell private/private-hosted options and want to evaluate Redwood as both a runtime partner and potential reseller integration.
[00:00:28] Liam: Liam, CTO. Focused on latency SLAs and cost predictability, and how this would fit in our cloud workflow.
[00:00:34] Jae: Jae, infra. I handle clusters, networking, and CI/CD for infra.
[00:00:38] Rana: Rana, security. I'll be focused on compliance and key management questions.
[00:00:42] Marco: Great, thanks. Quick agenda: 1) understand Hyperloom's customer use cases and constraints, 2) discuss Redwood's integration patterns (hosted, dedicated, private), 3) surface security/compliance, and 4) outline a pilot and next steps.

[00:01:05] Priya: Sounds good. To set context, our customers are fintech and healthcare SaaS vendors; many need data residency and strict audit logs. We offer a managed layer that brokers GPU capacity across partners and want to add inference as a first-class managed capability. Our questions: can Redwood run a hybrid model where we route traffic to our pools and to Redwood-hosted for burst? How does billing and routing work?
[00:01:34] Claire: Good question. In general, Redwood supports multi-mode deployments — hosted API for quick time-to-value, Dedicated pools for reserved capacity, and Private (VPC/on-prem) for strict isolation. For routing you can set policies by latency, cost, or region — and we can fall back to compatible model variants. For billing, there are a few partner flows: reseller (you resell capacity), referral, or we can do usage-based invoicing tied to your account. Tanya can run the commercial follow-up.

[00:02:05] Priya: Okay. For us the technical picture matters: we need prefix caching/KV cache support, and continuous batching on the serving side — otherwise our per-token cost is too high. Also, many customers use long context windows (8k+), and memory/KV handling is a concern.
[00:02:23] Marco: Understood. Our serving runtime supports KV caching and workload-aware batching; we have explicit controls for cache TTLs and per-route batch sizing. For long contexts we select kernels and quantization profiles to optimize memory usage; we can also recommend model variants that preserve quality at lower cost. Worth noting that very long KV-heavy sessions may still benefit from Dedicated capacity.

[00:02:55] Liam: What's the typical latency delta between Hosted versus Dedicated? Our SLOs are 95th <120ms and 99th <250ms for short chats (<=512 tokens) — is that realistic?
[00:03:08] Marco: Short answer: yes for Dedicated and in many cases for Hosted in close regions. Hosted has more multi-tenant variability, so Dedicated gives predictable 95/99 percentiles because you get reserved GPU pools and can tune batch sizes. We typically see sub-100ms medians on optimized models with small tokens in Dedicated. Hosted can hit your SLO if pinned to certain models and regions, but less guaranteed.

[00:03:34] Priya: Are there network-level implications? If we do VPC peering for Private deployments, do we see impacts on latency?
[00:03:40] Marco: VPC like private deployments add a small network hop; usually under 5-20ms depending on peering/latency to the region. The bigger delta is whether you're sharing GPUs vs reserved — that's where batching and queueing can add tail latency.

[00:03:58] Rana: Security questions: do you offer KMS integrations and HSM? We need to know encryption at rest, in transit, and key rotation controls for a private deployment. Also SOC 2, and can you surface audit logs for each inference request?
[00:04:12] Claire: Yes. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integration; hosted supports envelope encryption and our platform integrates with major KMS providers. We can provide SOC 2 reports and we have per-request audit logs; we'll share our security pack after this call.

[00:04:29] Rana: And SSO/SAML and RBAC?
[00:04:33] Marco: We have enterprise SSO via SAML and granular RBAC, and token-level scoping for operations and usage tracking.

[00:04:41] Jae: On integration, our current control plane is Kubernetes-based, and we deploy partner connectors in a separate namespace. Does Redwood provide an operator or helm chart for Private deployments?
[00:04:50] Marco: For Private we provide a customer-managed control plane package; it's distributed as Helm charts and an operator for lifecycle. For on-prem there is an air-gapped installer and guided support. For VPC, we have IaC templates (Terraform) that we can adapt.

[00:05:06] Priya: Good. Two other constraints: 1) we want to surface cost transparency to customers (per-route token breakdown), and 2) ability to pin model versions per customer tenant.
[00:05:16] Claire: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route/model. Pinning model versions per tenant is supported via our deployment abstraction — you can pin model versions and rollout policies per tenant.

[00:05:33] Liam: On the partner side, how would failover work? Example: if Dedicated pool is saturated, can traffic fallback to Redwood-hosted or another model variant automatically?
[00:05:42] Marco: Yes — smart routing policies can fallback by model variant, region, or cost tier. You can configure canary and automatic fallback to keep apps online. This is something we use in production for graceful degradation.

[00:06:00] Priya: For pilot scope, our ideal is: a 30-day pilot with two customer tenants, mixed traffic (chats + embeddings), run Redwood on a Dedicated pool and route overflow to Hosted. We'll want a benchmark window with synthetic and sampled customer traffic. Is that feasible?
[00:06:17] Claire: Totally feasible. Typical pilot steps: 1) agree on traffic profiles and models, 2) provision Dedicated pool and access, 3) run benchmark window (we'll coordinate with Marco), 4) evaluate cost/latency and share results and then decide on go-to-market model. Tanya: commercial options?
[00:06:33] Tanya: From partner perspective we can do several go-to-market models — referral fee, reseller margin, or co-sell where Redwood invoices end customers. We'll follow up with a short partner commercial template.

[00:06:46] Rana: About data residency — some of our customers require that data never leaves EU. How does Redwood ensure regional isolation?
[00:06:54] Marco: We can pin deployments to specific regions and also run Private clusters in your VPC/region for full control. Hosted can be regional but if legal requirements demand customer-managed infrastructure we'd recommend Private.

[00:07:07] Priya: What about model artifacts? Some customers want models hosted by us; can we bring-your-own-model (BYOM) and run it on Redwood Dedicated?
[00:07:14] Marco: Yes. BYOM is supported for Dedicated and Private deployments. We have onboarding steps for model packaging and perf profiling; we'll need weights, model config, and a small test harness to run perf tests.

[00:07:24] Liam: Pricing question — how do quantization recommendations affect licensing or accuracy guarantees?
[00:07:30] Marco: Quantization is a runtime profile option; it typically reduces cost with small impacts on output quality depending on model. We run evals against your prompt sets to ensure regression doesn't exceed your thresholds. Licensing for models depends on the model's license; for open models there's no additional licensing, but for commercial models we'd surface terms.

[00:07:49] Priya: Can Redwood provide a list of pre-verified models and perf profiles?
[00:07:52] Claire: We maintain a model catalog with Redwood-verified performance profiles and recommended quantization/sequence settings. We'll include a subset relevant to your use cases in the security/commercial pack.

[00:08:05] Jae: On telemetry: we need tracing hooks and per-route dashboards so our ops team can correlate traces to our existing APM. Do you support OpenTelemetry?
[00:08:13] Marco: Yes — we support OpenTelemetry tracing hooks and export to common backends. The Console supports per-route dashboards and tracing links.

[00:08:22] Priya: Ok that's promising. A couple of gotchas we've run into with other vendors: 1) hidden egress costs when routing to hosted endpoints, and 2) poor support for long-running KV sessions which blow up memory. Do you have recommended mitigations?
[00:08:36] Marco: For egress we can do regional placement and VPC peering to minimize cross-provider egress. For KV, we recommend TTL policies and periodic snapshotting for very long contexts; for extremely long-lived sessions Dedicated with tuned cache sizes helps. We'll surface recommended batch and cache configs once we see your sample traces.

[00:08:58] Liam: Who else from Redwood will we be working with during pilot?
[00:09:02] Claire: Marco will lead the technical deep dive and benchmarks. Tanya will manage partner commercial terms. I will be primary account lead. We'll also loop in Solutions Engineering and an engagement manager for Dedicated provisioning.

[00:09:14] Priya: Timeline-wise, if we start provisioning next week could we be running benchmarks by mid-December? Our Q1 rollouts depend on pilot results.
[00:09:22] Marco: Yes — if we get sample traffic and model artifacts this week, we can schedule a benchmark window in ~10 days. That would push results mid-December.

[00:09:34] Claire: Quick recap and open issues: 1) Redwood to share security pack (SOC2, KMS notes, audit log examples), 2) Hyperloom to share traffic profiles and which customers/tenants for pilot, 3) Marco to schedule deep dive and benchmark. Agreed?
[00:09:48] Priya: Agreed.
[00:09:50] Rana: Agreed.
[00:09:52] Liam: Agreed.

[00:09:55] --- Transcript body (detailed) ---
[00:10:00] Speaker 1: so one quick note, sorry liao, that we also wanna make sure that the compliance reviewers at each customer can access a read-only audit view, like a "per-tenant audit". Is that a thing?
[00:10:15] Marco: Yes it's possible to scope audit logs per tenant and we can provide read-only dashboards or export them to your SIEM. There might be retention costs depending on retention length.
[00:10:27] Priya: Good — retention policies per customer are a hard requirement for some of our healthcare customers.
[00:10:31] Claire: We'll add retention policy options in the pack.
[00:10:34] Jae: On the helm/operator side, do you have a GitOps-friendly workflow? We run ArgoCD.
[00:10:40] Marco: We support GitOps — Helm chart values and a sample ArgoCD app manifest are part of the Private install. We'll share those artifacts.
[00:10:48] Priya: Another concern: what happens to KV caches on failover? If we fail to Hosted, do we lose session context?
[00:10:56] Marco: If you fail between Dedicated and Hosted, you'd likely lose in-memory KV cache; we recommend prefix caching with periodic Durability snapshots for critical sessions, or route sticky sessions to keep KV locality. We can co-design the strategy.
[00:11:12] Priya: Hmm, ok. We'll need guidance on session durability patterns.
[00:11:17] Marco: We'll prepare a short doc on durability and sticky routing patterns.
[00:11:21] Tanya: On partner economics — early pilots often go as 'cost+ pilot' where we provide discounted Dedicated units and we measure unit economics then decide on reseller/referral. We'll propose a 60-day evaluation commercial template.
[00:11:34] Liam: From a legal/procurement perspective, we may need a data processing addendum and specific SLAs. Do you have standard templates?
[00:11:41] Claire: Yes, we have standard DPA and SLA templates we can circulate. For enterprise deals we customize. We'll include drafts in the security/commercial zip.
[00:11:51] Priya: Regarding model BYO — are there any constraints on model size or license that would block running on Redwood?
[00:11:57] Marco: For model size, constraints depend on GPU type and quantization. We support models up to multi-billion parameters; larger models may require model sharding. For licenses, some commercial model licenses forbid hosting or redistribution; we audit and flag any licensing restrictions.
[00:12:14] Priya: Perfect.
[00:12:16] Claire: Anything else on the architectural side?
[00:12:18] Jae: Not right now. We'll gather sample traces and model artifacts.
[00:12:22] Rana: Security folks will follow up with a short questionnaire.
[00:12:26] Claire: Great. We'll compile the pack and send a calendar invite for the deep dive.

[00:12:33] --- Closing ---
[00:12:35] Claire: Thanks everyone. Next steps: I will send the security/commercial pack, Marco will set up the deep dive, Priya and team will share traffic samples. I'll ping for dates and follow up with Tanya on partner terms.
[00:12:49] Priya: Thanks all.
[00:12:51] Liam: Thanks.
[00:12:52] Marco: Thanks, bye.

[00:12:55] End of recording.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-attr (Speaker 1) and minor words misheard; placeholders used where participant interrupted.
